stem: The Indus Valley Civilisation is also known as the:
solution: It is called the Harappan Civilisation after Harappa, the first site to be discovered. It is also called the Sindhu–Sarasvati Civilisation.

stem: In terms of metal use, the Harappan Civilisation belonged to the:
solution: The Harappans used bronze (an alloy of copper and tin), placing their civilisation in the Bronze Age.

stem: The famous 'Great Bath' was discovered at which Harappan site?
solution: The Great Bath, a large watertight tank, was found at Mohenjo-daro (in present-day Pakistan).

stem: The Harappan site of Lothal, known for a dockyard, is located in the present-day state of:
solution: Lothal, with its famous dockyard indicating maritime trade, is in Gujarat.

stem: Rakhigarhi, one of the largest Harappan sites, is located in which state?
solution: Rakhigarhi, among the largest sites of the civilisation, lies in Haryana.

stem: The city of Mohenjo-daro was situated on the banks of which river?
solution: Mohenjo-daro stood on the Indus (Sindhu). Harappa, by contrast, was on the river Ravi.

stem: Which feature best characterises Harappan town planning?
options: A grid pattern of streets with a covered drainage system
solution: Harappan cities had streets laid out in a grid, crossing at right angles, with an advanced covered drainage system.

stem: A notable unresolved feature of the Harappan Civilisation is that its:
options: Script has not yet been deciphered
solution: The Harappan script, found mainly on seals, remains undeciphered to this day.

stem: The Harappan site of Dholavira, famed for its water-management systems, is located in:
solution: Dholavira, known for sophisticated reservoirs and water conservation, is in the Rann of Kutch region of Gujarat.

stem: Harappan seals were most commonly made of which material?
solution: Most Harappan seals were carved from steatite (soapstone), often engraved with animals such as the 'unicorn' and undeciphered script.

stem: The Harappan Civilisation was first brought to light by excavations in which decade?
solution: Harappa and Mohenjo-daro were excavated in the 1920s, revealing the civilisation to the modern world.

stem: The uniform, standardised bricks and weights across Harappan cities suggest:
options: A high degree of standardisation and central regulation
That each house made its own random measures
solution: Standardised baked bricks (in fixed ratios) and cubical stone weights point to remarkable standardisation and organised civic control across the civilisation.

stem: The first Harappan site to be discovered, which gave the civilisation its name, was:
solution: HARAPPA (on the river Ravi) was the FIRST site to be discovered, which is why the civilisation is called the HARAPPAN Civilisation. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The Harappan Civilisation is also called the Sindhu–Sarasvati Civilisation because many sites were found along the:
options: Indus (Sindhu) and the dried-up Sarasvati river beds
solution: It is called the SINDHU–SARASVATI Civilisation because many sites lay along the INDUS (SINDHU) and the (now largely dried-up) SARASVATI river beds. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Harappan cities were typically divided into two parts: a higher fortified area and a lower area. The higher part is called the:
solution: Harappan cities usually had a higher, fortified western part called the CITADEL (housing important structures) and a LOWER TOWN (residential area) to the east. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The Harappans were among the earliest people in the world to grow and use:
solution: The Harappans were among the EARLIEST people to grow COTTON and make cloth from it — cotton was a major Harappan contribution. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The famous bronze figurine known as the 'Dancing Girl' was found at:
solution: The bronze 'DANCING GIRL' figurine, made by the lost-wax method, was found at MOHENJO-DARO. It shows the Harappans' skill in metal casting. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The Harappan drainage system is remarkable because:
options: Drains were covered and ran along the streets, connected to house drains
There were no drains at all
solution: The Harappan DRAINAGE SYSTEM is remarkable because DRAINS were COVERED and ran along the streets, CONNECTED to drains from individual houses — showing advanced sanitation and civic planning. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Harappan houses commonly had which of the following?
options: No connection to the street drains
solution: Harappan HOUSES commonly had their own WELLS, BATHROOMS, and COVERED DRAINS connected to the street drainage — reflecting a high standard of civic and personal hygiene. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The Harappan site of Kalibangan, known for ploughed field evidence and fire altars, is in which state?
solution: KALIBANGAN, famous for evidence of a PLOUGHED FIELD and FIRE ALTARS, is located in RAJASTHAN. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Harappan seals often depict which animal, along with the undeciphered script?
solution: Harappan SEALS often depict a 'UNICORN'-like ONE-HORNED animal (as well as bulls, elephants, and rhinoceroses), along with the undeciphered Harappan script. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Evidence of Harappan trade with distant lands includes contact with:
options: Mesopotamia (where Harappan seals have been found)
solution: Harappan trade reached MESOPOTAMIA — Harappan-type seals and goods have been found there, and Mesopotamian texts refer to trade with 'Meluhha' (thought to be the Harappan region). So option 1 is correct.

stem: In Mesopotamian records, the Harappan region is believed to have been referred to as:
solution: Mesopotamian records refer to a trading land called MELUHHA, which scholars believe was the HARAPPAN region — evidence of long-distance trade. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The Harappans were skilled crafts-people, especially in making:
options: Beads, pottery, and objects of metal and stone
solution: The Harappans were skilled in making BEADS (of carnelian and other stones), POTTERY, and objects of METAL and STONE — their bead-making and craft work were highly developed. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The large brick structure at some Harappan sites, thought to store grain, is called a:
solution: The large brick structures thought to STORE GRAIN at Harappan sites (like Harappa and Mohenjo-daro) are called GRANARIES. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Which of the following metals did the Harappans NOT use?
solution: The Harappans did NOT use IRON (iron came into wide use later, in the Iron Age). They used COPPER, BRONZE, GOLD, and silver. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The Great Bath at Mohenjo-daro is believed to have been used for:
solution: The GREAT BATH — a large, watertight tank with steps — is believed to have been used for RITUAL BATHING or CEREMONIAL purposes, showing the importance of water and cleanliness. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The Harappan Civilisation flourished roughly during which period?
solution: The mature HARAPPAN Civilisation flourished roughly between 2600 and 1900 BCE — making it one of the world's oldest urban civilisations. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Consider the pairs: 1. Great Bath — Mohenjo-daro 2. Dockyard — Lothal 3. Water reservoirs — Dholavira. How many pairs are correctly matched?
solution: ALL THREE pairs are correct: the GREAT BATH is at MOHENJO-DARO; the DOCKYARD is at LOTHAL; and the famous WATER RESERVOIRS are at DHOLAVIRA. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The Harappan weights were made in a fixed system, mostly using:
options: A binary/doubling and decimal scheme with cubical stone weights
solution: Harappan WEIGHTS were CUBICAL stone weights made in a FIXED SYSTEM (following a doubling and decimal pattern), showing standardisation across the civilisation for trade. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The dockyard at Lothal indicates that the Harappans engaged in:
solution: The DOCKYARD at LOTHAL indicates that the Harappans engaged in MARITIME (SEA) TRADE, using boats to carry goods along the coast and to distant lands. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Why is the Harappan Civilisation considered an 'urban' civilisation?
options: It had well-planned cities with streets, drains, and civic amenities
solution: The Harappan Civilisation is considered URBAN because it had WELL-PLANNED CITIES with grid STREETS, covered DRAINS, wells, granaries, and civic amenities — the hallmarks of city life. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The Harappan script is written in which direction (as seen on seals)?
options: Generally right to left (boustrophedon in some cases)
Only top to bottom in English
Only left to right like English
solution: The HARAPPAN SCRIPT was generally written from RIGHT to LEFT (and sometimes in boustrophedon, alternating directions). It remains undeciphered. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Which of the following is a possible reason suggested for the decline of the Harappan Civilisation?
options: Climate change, drying of rivers, floods, or shifts in trade
A single volcano destroying everything overnight
solution: Possible reasons suggested for the DECLINE of the Harappan Civilisation include CLIMATE CHANGE, the DRYING of RIVERS (like the Sarasvati), FLOODS, and SHIFTS in TRADE — likely a combination of factors rather than one cause. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Which crops were commonly grown by the Harappans?
options: Wheat, barley, and pulses (and they knew cotton)
solution: The Harappans commonly grew WHEAT, BARLEY, and PULSES (as well as sesame and cotton). (Maize and potato came to India much later, from the Americas.) So option 1 is correct.

stem: The stone statue often called the 'Priest-King' was found at:
solution: The famous stone bust known as the 'PRIEST-KING', wearing a decorated robe, was found at MOHENJO-DARO. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The Harappan Civilisation extended over parts of present-day:
solution: The Harappan Civilisation was VAST, extending over parts of present-day INDIA, PAKISTAN, and AFGHANISTAN — one of the largest ancient civilisations in area. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Assertion (A): The Harappans had an advanced sense of town planning. Reason (R): Their cities had grid-pattern streets, covered drains, and standardised bricks. Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
solution: A is TRUE — the Harappans had advanced town planning. R is TRUE and correctly EXPLAINS A: their cities had GRID-PATTERN STREETS, COVERED DRAINS, and STANDARDISED BRICKS, which are precisely the features that demonstrate advanced planning. So R is the correct explanation of A. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Harappan bricks were notable for being:
options: Baked (kiln-fired) and made in a fixed size ratio
Different random sizes in every city
solution: Harappan BRICKS were notable for being BAKED (kiln-fired) and made in a FIXED SIZE RATIO (length:width:height of about 4:2:1) — used uniformly across cities, showing standardisation. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Which of the following shows the Harappans' skill in water management?
options: Reservoirs and dams at Dholavira and wells across cities
The complete absence of water use
Living only in deserts with no water
solution: The Harappans' skill in WATER MANAGEMENT is shown by the RESERVOIRS and DAMS at DHOLAVIRA and the many WELLS across their cities — sophisticated methods to store and supply water. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Rakhigarhi and Dholavira are important because they show that:
options: Many major Harappan sites lie within present-day India
The civilisation was only in one small area
solution: RAKHIGARHI (Haryana) and DHOLAVIRA (Gujarat) are important because they show that MANY MAJOR Harappan sites lie within PRESENT-DAY INDIA, not only across the border. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Which statement about the Harappan people's religion/beliefs is supported by evidence?
options: Seals, figurines and structures suggest they revered certain animals, a mother-goddess figure, and water
They had no beliefs at all
They left no clues about beliefs
solution: Evidence such as SEALS, terracotta FIGURINES (including a possible MOTHER-GODDESS), and the GREAT BATH suggests the Harappans REVERED certain ANIMALS, a mother-goddess figure, and WATER/cleanliness. (Since the script is undeciphered, much remains uncertain.) So option 1 is correct.

stem: The Harappan Civilisation is one of the world's ancient civilisations, alongside those of:
solution: The Harappan Civilisation is one of the world's OLDEST, alongside the ancient civilisations of MESOPOTAMIA, EGYPT, and CHINA. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The Harappan practice of making objects from carnelian, agate and other stones shows their expertise in:
solution: Making objects from CARNELIAN, AGATE, and other stones shows the Harappans' expertise in BEAD-MAKING and STONE-CRAFT — their beads were traded far and wide. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Which of the following correctly pairs a Harappan site with its modern location?
options: Lothal → Gujarat; Kalibangan → Rajasthan; Rakhigarhi → Haryana
Lothal → Punjab; Kalibangan → Kerala; Rakhigarhi → Tamil Nadu
solution: The correct pairings are: LOTHAL → GUJARAT; KALIBANGAN → RAJASTHAN; and RAKHIGARHI → HARYANA. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The absence of large palaces or grand royal tombs in Harappan cities suggests that:
options: Their society may not have had the kind of powerful kings seen in some other civilisations
They had no organisation at all
solution: The ABSENCE of large PALACES or grand royal TOMBS suggests the Harappan society may NOT have had the kind of powerful, dominant KINGS seen in Egypt or Mesopotamia — how it was governed remains debated. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Terracotta (baked clay) objects found at Harappan sites include:
options: Toys, figurines, and models of carts
solution: TERRACOTTA (baked clay) objects at Harappan sites include TOYS, FIGURINES (of humans and animals), and models of CARTS — revealing everyday life and children's play. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The Harappans obtained raw materials like copper, gold and precious stones through:
options: Trade and procurement from different regions
solution: The Harappans obtained raw materials like COPPER, GOLD, and PRECIOUS STONES through TRADE and PROCUREMENT from DIFFERENT REGIONS (e.g., copper from Rajasthan, gold and stones from various areas) — a wide trading network. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The Harappan Civilisation matters to Indian history because it shows that:
options: India had a highly developed urban civilisation thousands of years ago
Cities were unknown in ancient India
solution: The Harappan Civilisation matters because it shows that INDIA had a HIGHLY DEVELOPED URBAN CIVILISATION — with planned cities, trade, crafts, and writing — THOUSANDS of YEARS AGO. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The overall message of the chapter 'The Beginnings of Indian Civilisation' is that:
options: The HARAPPAN (Sindhu–Sarasvati) Civilisation — one of the world's oldest, flourishing around 2600–1900 BCE across parts of India, Pakistan and Afghanistan — was a remarkable BRONZE AGE URBAN civilisation with well-planned cities (citadel and lower town, grid streets, covered drains, wells, granaries), standardised baked bricks and weights, skilled crafts (beads, pottery, metalwork, cotton cloth), long-distance trade (with Mesopotamia/Meluhha), famous sites like Mohenjo-daro, Harappa, Dholavira, Lothal and Rakhigarhi, and an as-yet undeciphered script — revealing that India had a highly advanced civilisation thousands of years ago
solution: The chapter's overall message is that the HARAPPAN (Sindhu–Sarasvati) Civilisation — one of the WORLD's OLDEST, flourishing around 2600–1900 BCE across parts of INDIA, PAKISTAN, and AFGHANISTAN — was a remarkable BRONZE AGE URBAN civilisation. It had WELL-PLANNED CITIES (with a CITADEL and LOWER TOWN, GRID STREETS, COVERED DRAINS, WELLS, and GRANARIES), STANDARDISED baked BRICKS and cubical WEIGHTS, SKILLED CRAFTS (beads, pottery, metalwork, and cotton cloth), and LONG-DISTANCE TRADE (reaching MESOPOTAMIA, the 'Meluhha' of their records). Famous sites include MOHENJO-DARO (Great Bath, Dancing Girl, Priest-King), HARAPPA, DHOLAVIRA (water reservoirs), LOTHAL (dockyard), and RAKHIGARHI. Its SCRIPT remains UNDECIPHERED. All this reveals that India had a HIGHLY ADVANCED civilisation thousands of years ago. So the overall message is option 2.

stem: The Harappan Civilisation belongs to which age?
solution: The Harappan Civilisation was a Bronze Age civilisation (c. 2600–1900 BCE), one of the world's earliest urban civilisations along with Mesopotamia and Egypt.

stem: Which of the following was a major Harappan site located in present-day Pakistan on the Ravi river?
solution: Harappa, on the Ravi river in Punjab (Pakistan), was the first Indus site excavated and gives the civilisation its alternative name.

stem: 'Mohenjo-daro', a major Harappan city, is located on the banks of the:
solution: Mohenjo-daro ('Mound of the Dead') lies on the Indus river in Sindh (Pakistan); it is famous for the Great Bath and an advanced drainage system.

stem: Lothal, a Harappan site known for its dockyard, is located in the present-day state of:
solution: Lothal in Gujarat had an artificial dockyard, indicating that the Harappans engaged in maritime trade.

stem: Dholavira, a major Harappan city known for its water management, is located in:
solution: Dholavira in the Rann of Kutch, Gujarat, is famous for its sophisticated water conservation system and is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

stem: The Harappan cities are noted for their well-planned layout with:
options: A grid pattern of streets and an advanced covered drainage system
solution: Harappan cities featured a grid layout with streets crossing at right angles and a remarkable underground/covered drainage system — hallmarks of advanced town planning.

stem: Harappan cities were typically divided into two parts: a raised 'citadel' and a:
solution: Harappan cities generally had a raised citadel (with important structures) to the west and a lower town (residential area) to the east.

stem: The Harappan script:
solution: The Harappan script, found mainly on seals, remains undeciphered; it was written mostly from right to left (boustrophedon in places).

stem: Harappan seals were commonly made of:
solution: Most Harappan seals were made of steatite (soapstone) and often depicted animals like the humped bull and the 'unicorn', along with script.

stem: The most famous Harappan seal, depicting a figure surrounded by animals, is called the:
solution: The 'Pashupati seal' from Mohenjo-daro shows a seated figure surrounded by animals, interpreted by some as a proto-Shiva (Pashupati, lord of animals).

stem: The bronze figurine known as the 'Dancing Girl' was found at:
solution: The 'Dancing Girl', a famous bronze statuette made using the lost-wax (cire perdue) technique, was found at Mohenjo-daro, showing Harappan metallurgical skill.

stem: The Harappans did NOT have knowledge of which metal?
solution: The Harappans used copper, bronze, gold and silver, but they did not know iron — iron came into use in India only later, in the Vedic/Iron Age.

stem: The chief crops grown by the Harappans included wheat, barley and:
options: Rice (in some areas), peas and sesame
solution: Harappans cultivated wheat, barley, peas, sesame and, in some regions, rice; cotton was also grown — India was among the first to grow cotton.

stem: Kalibangan, a Harappan site known for ploughed fields, is located in:
solution: Kalibangan in Rajasthan is notable for evidence of the earliest ploughed agricultural field and fire altars.

stem: The Harappan economy was significantly based on:
options: Agriculture, craft production and trade (including long-distance trade)
solution: The Harappan economy rested on agriculture, craft production (beads, pottery, metalwork) and extensive trade, including with Mesopotamia (called 'Meluhha').

stem: The Harappans traded with Mesopotamia, where their land was referred to as:
solution: Mesopotamian records refer to the Harappan region as 'Meluhha', indicating flourishing long-distance maritime trade between the two civilisations.

stem: Harappans used a system of standardised weights and measures based on the ratio:
solution: Harappan weights followed a binary system in the lower values (1, 2, 4, 8, 16...) and were remarkably standardised, indicating regulated trade.

stem: The decline of the Harappan Civilisation (around 1900 BCE) is attributed to factors such as:
options: Climate change, drying of rivers, floods and possible ecological/other factors
solution: The decline is attributed to multiple possible factors — climate change, the drying/shifting of rivers (like the Saraswati/Ghaggar-Hakra), floods, deforestation and disruption of trade — rather than one cause.

stem: The prehistoric period before the invention of writing is called the:
solution: The prehistoric period refers to the time before written records; history is reconstructed from it through archaeological evidence like tools and fossils.

stem: The earliest period of human history, characterised by the use of rough stone tools, is the:
solution: The Palaeolithic (Old Stone Age) is the earliest period, when humans were hunter-gatherers using rough, chipped stone tools.

stem: The Neolithic (New Stone Age) is significant because it saw the beginning of:
options: Agriculture and domestication of animals (and settled life)
solution: The Neolithic Revolution saw humans begin farming and domesticating animals, leading to settled village life, pottery and polished stone tools — a turning point in human history.

stem: Mehrgarh, one of the earliest Neolithic sites in the subcontinent showing early farming, is in present-day:
solution: Mehrgarh in Balochistan (Pakistan) is one of the earliest known Neolithic farming settlements in the subcontinent, predating the Harappan cities.

stem: Prehistoric rock paintings depicting hunting scenes are famously found at:
solution: The rock shelters of Bhimbetka in Madhya Pradesh, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, contain prehistoric paintings depicting hunting, dancing and daily life.

stem: The 'Chalcolithic' period is named for the use of which two materials?
solution: The Chalcolithic ('copper-stone') period saw the use of copper alongside stone tools, bridging the Neolithic and the full Bronze/Iron ages.

stem: Which of the following is considered evidence used by archaeologists to study early civilisations?
options: Artefacts, tools, pottery, seals, bones and structures
solution: Archaeologists study material remains — tools, pottery, seals, ornaments, bones, buildings — to reconstruct the life of early peoples, especially for prehistoric times without writing.

stem: The Harappan Civilisation was spread over parts of present-day:
solution: The Harappan Civilisation extended across present-day Pakistan, north-western and western India (Punjab, Haryana, Rajasthan, Gujarat) and parts of Afghanistan — a very large area.

stem: Rakhigarhi, one of the largest Harappan sites, is located in the Indian state of:
solution: Rakhigarhi in Haryana is one of the largest Harappan sites and among the biggest in the Indian subcontinent, important for recent archaeological and DNA studies.

stem: A distinctive feature of Harappan society, based on archaeological evidence, is that:
options: There were grand temples and palaces like Egypt
No large temples or palaces have been clearly identified, suggesting a distinctive social order
solution: Unlike Egypt or Mesopotamia, no clearly identifiable grand temples, palaces or royal tombs have been found at Harappan sites, suggesting a society organised differently, with an emphasis on civic planning.

stem: The 'Priest-King', a famous Harappan sculpture, was found at:
solution: The steatite bust known as the 'Priest-King', wearing a decorated robe, was found at Mohenjo-daro; its exact significance remains uncertain.

stem: Cotton cultivation and textile production were notable in the Harappan Civilisation; the Greeks later called cotton:
solution: The Harappans were among the earliest to grow and weave cotton; the Greeks called it 'sindon', derived from Sindh, reflecting the region's association with cotton.

stem: The main occupation of most Harappan people was:
solution: Most Harappans were farmers and herders; agriculture and animal husbandry supported the cities, while artisans and traders formed other important sections of society.

stem: Which river, now largely dried up, is associated with many Harappan sites and mentioned in later texts?
solution: Many Harappan sites lie along the now largely dry Ghaggar-Hakra river system, often identified with the ancient Saraswati mentioned in later Vedic texts.

stem: The study of the past through the excavation and analysis of material remains is called:
solution: Archaeology is the study of the human past through the excavation and analysis of material remains — artefacts, structures and other physical evidence.

stem: Harappan children's toys and games found by archaeologists indicate that the civilisation had:
options: A developed social and cultural life, including recreation
solution: Finds of toy carts, whistles, marbles and dice show that Harappans had leisure and a developed social/cultural life beyond mere survival.

stem: The term used for the earliest, mature and late phases of the Harappan Civilisation reflects that it:
options: Developed gradually over stages (Early, Mature, Late Harappan)
solution: The Harappan Civilisation is divided into Early (developing), Mature (urban, c. 2600–1900 BCE) and Late (declining) phases, showing gradual growth and decline.

stem: Which of the following statements about the Harappan Civilisation is correct? (i) It had advanced town planning (ii) Its script is undeciphered (iii) It knew the use of iron
solution: Statements (i) and (ii) are correct — advanced town planning and an undeciphered script. Statement (iii) is wrong: the Harappans did NOT know iron.
